newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Transpower ups guard against NZ power shortfalls.
newsitem.headline: Transpower ups guard against NZ power shortfalls.

text.p: New Zealand's national grid operator Transpower will improve its security measures from Friday after available power supply was twice stretched to near critical levels in the new wholesale electricity market.

Chief executive Bob Thomson said Transpower had considered invoking security measures on October 15 and November 2, when actual electricity demand had substantially exceeded market forecasts. The amount of generation capacity on offer had bordered on the critically low.
"On the 15th of October and the 2nd of November we seriously thought about invoking security," Thomson told Reuters.
"Now we've put a measure in to stop that. We've put an information measure in so that we don't have to invoke it and we can warn everybody well ahead."
He said electricity demand forecasts in the new wholesale market, launched on October 1, were falling about 10 percent short of actual demand.

The new system will add a 10 percent safety margin to demand estimates from the market and reserves on top of that, effectively lowering the threshold at which Transpower is alerted to a possible shortfall in generation capacity.
"What it actually does is tells the market that we see problems coming and it then gives them time to react to increase the volume. We'll get more security and so will they," Thomson said.

While Transpower was concerned only with volume, and not with prices, the new measure would serve to reduce the severity of spikes in the spot price of electricity which occurred as a result of misforecast demand.
When severe anomalies between actual and forecast demand occurred, more expensive generation plant than expected had to be run, resulting in a price spike.
Price spikes have plagued the market in its first month of operation. Market operator EMCO has indentified three causes of the spikes, and two have been eliminated from invoices to retailers.
But those which occurred as a result of inaccurate demand forecasts will stand.
"Certainly there is a considerable urgency in ensuring the regular and continued accuracy of the forecast quantities," EMCO Chief Executive Lincoln Gould said on Tuesday.
